items.title: The Sleepy Rabbit
items.passage:
Theo had tied the same knot eleven times, and eleven times it had slid apart when Aunt Rosa tugged the rope.

"The rabbit comes up out of the hole," she said, tapping the loop he had made. "Around the tree, and back down the hole."

Theo frowned at the rope. His rabbit kept going down the wrong hole. Out on the lake, the little sailboat bumped against the dock as if it were tired of waiting.

On the twelfth try, he went slowly. Up through the loop. Around the long end of the rope. Back down. When Aunt Rosa pulled, the knot tightened and held.

"Now you can tie up the boat," she said.

That afternoon his younger sister, Mia, sat on the dock with a piece of string and a scowl. "Show me," she said.

Theo started to say, "Up, around, down," very fast, the way he said it in his head. Mia's string flopped into a tangle. He stopped. He remembered the eleven knots that had slid apart and the way Aunt Rosa had waited beside him without a single sigh.

"Okay," he said, sitting down next to her. "The rabbit lives in this hole. Go slow. It's a sleepy rabbit."

Mia giggled. On her fourth try, the knot held. She held it up like a prize, and Theo found that he was prouder of her knot than he had been of his own.

distractor_rationales.reason: "He doubts that Mia is old enough to learn the knot." has no support; Theo never questions Mia's age, and she ties the knot on her fourth try.

distractor_rationales.choice: He wants to impress Aunt Rosa by teaching Mia well.

items.title: Operation Breakfast
items.passage:
Nora and Sam had a plan for their mother's birthday, and the plan had a name: Operation Breakfast.

At 5:30 in the morning, they crept into the kitchen in their socks. Sam was in charge of toast. Nora was in charge of pancakes, because she had watched a cooking show twice.

The first pancake stuck to the pan. The second one flipped so high that it landed on top of the refrigerator. Biscuit, the dog, sat below it with great hope.

"Toast is easy," Sam whispered, and he pushed the lever down. Then he pushed it down again, to be safe.

A thin gray curl of smoke rose from the toaster. Then the smoke alarm began to shriek.

Biscuit barked. Nora dropped the spatula. Sam waved a dish towel at the ceiling as if he were signaling a ship.

Upstairs, a door opened. Their mother appeared in the kitchen doorway in her bathrobe, blinking at the haze, the batter on the floor, and the pancake on the refrigerator.

"Happy birthday!" the twins shouted.

For a moment she said nothing at all. Then she laughed so hard she had to sit down. She opened the window, rescued the pan, and made three perfect pancakes in about two minutes.

"This," she said, handing them each a plate, "is the best birthday breakfast anyone has ever made me."

"You made it," Sam pointed out.

"I know," said their mother. "That's what makes it funny."

distractor_rationales.reason: "to explain why their mother wakes up before the smoke alarm sounds" is contradicted by the order of events: the alarm shrieks first, and only then does a door open upstairs.

distractor_rationales.choice: to suggest that the toaster in the house is already broken

items.title: A Muffled Clue
items.passage:
Ten minutes before the spring concert, Ms. Alvarez's harmonica was gone.

She played it for one short solo in the middle of the second song. She always left it on the music stand beside her chair, resting on top of its little blue case. June, who played the tuba, sat in the chair right next to hers.

"It was right here during warm-ups," Ms. Alvarez said. The case was there. The harmonica was not.

The band members searched their pockets and their folders. Dev, who played trombone, checked under the risers. Lena checked the hallway.

While the others searched, June ran through her warm-up notes. They came out thick and dull, like someone humming into a pillow. She tried again. The same dull sound.

June frowned. Her tuba had sounded bright and loud an hour ago. She remembered what had happened right after warm-ups: Dev had tripped on a cable and bumped into the music stands, and everything on them had rattled and bounced.

June turned the tuba upside down over a chair cushion and gave it a gentle shake. Something slid through the curving tubes, clicked against the brass, and dropped onto the cushion.

It was the harmonica.

"It must have bounced into the bell," June said. "My tuba was trying to tell us."

Ms. Alvarez laughed and wiped the harmonica on her sleeve. "Then your tuba has earned a solo of its own."

items.title: Seven O'Clock, Alder Street
items.passage:
At seven the street is still a held breath.
The shutters are down, gray as closed eyes,
and the sidewalk keeps last night's rain
in every crack like a secret.

Then the first one goes up with a rattle:
the florist, hauling her steel door
toward the sky, and behind it,
buckets of tulips leaning out to look.

The tailor follows, slower, one hand
on his back, one hand on the chain.
The newsstand unfolds its wooden wings.
The cafe drags out four small tables
and sets a chair beside each one
as if expecting old friends.

By eight the street has opened
every eye it has.
It is talking now in bells and voices,
in coins, in the hiss of the coffee machine,
and nobody remembers
that an hour ago
it was quiet enough
to hear the rain still dripping
from the tailor's awning,
one drop,
one drop,
one drop.

"Headman," she said, "your great pot is too tall for an old goat. If I could only drink from it, I would tell every traveler that the wisest man in the hills lives in Tarrow Ford."

Orrin liked the sound of that. He tipped his giant pot so that Pell could reach it. But it was so heavy that once it began to lean, it would not stop. Over it went, and the water rushed down the lane, filling every small pot on its way.

items.passage:
The winter I was eleven, my grandmother taught me to fold a paper crane, and it took me nine days.

She kept a stack of square paper in a tin that had once held buttons. Every afternoon, while my parents were still at work, she set two squares on the kitchen table: one for her and one for me.

Her hands moved the way water moves, smoothly and without a pause. Mine moved like a car in traffic. I folded corners unevenly, creased the wrong side, and once tore the neck clean off.

"Again," she said, sliding me a fresh square.

I wanted her to fold it for me. I said so on the fourth day, and she shook her head. "Then it would be my crane," she said, "and you would still have empty hands."

On the ninth day, I made one that stood up. Its wings were crooked, and one side of its tail was fatter than the other, but it stood on the table on its own two points and did not fall over.

My grandmother picked it up and turned it in the light the way a jeweler looks at a stone. Then she set it on the windowsill above the sink, where she kept the things she meant to keep forever.

She has been gone for three years now. I fold cranes for my little cousins when they visit, and they tear the necks off, and I slide them fresh squares. "Again," I say, and I hear her voice when I say it. The crooked crane is still on the windowsill. My mother has never moved it.

"Good afternoon, Kai," it said when I opened it in the cafeteria. "Today you have a turkey sandwich, carrot sticks, and an apple. Enjoy your balanced meal."

I glared at the lunchbox on the counter. It glowed a calm blue.

The Inca Empire stretched along the mountains of western South America in the 1400s and early 1500s, and it ran one of the largest states of its time. An empty space on the cord stands for zero.

Reading and making khipus was a job for trained record keepers, called khipukamayuq. Spanish writers who arrived in the 1500s described these keepers reciting long accounts, and even histories, from their cords.

That detail is one reason some researchers suspect that khipus recorded more than numbers: perhaps names, places, or even stories. So far, nobody has been able to prove it. Several hundred khipus survive in museums today, and scholars are still working to read the ones whose knots seem to break the rules of the number system.

items.title: Garrett Morgan's Pause
items.passage:
Garrett Morgan had only an elementary school education, but he had a mind that kept asking how things could work better.

Morgan was born in Kentucky in 1877, the son of parents who had been enslaved. As a teenager he moved north to Ohio, eventually settling in Cleveland, where he found work repairing sewing machines. He was good at it, and he was curious. Within a few years he had opened his own repair shop and later a clothing business.

His most dramatic invention was a breathing device he called a safety hood. The wearer pulled a canvas hood over the head, and a long tube hanging down drew in air from near the ground, where smoke is usually thinner. Morgan patented the hood in 1914 and showed how it worked by walking into tents filled with thick smoke.

In 1916, an explosion trapped workers in a tunnel being dug under Lake Erie. Morgan and his brother put on safety hoods, went into the tunnel, and helped carry men out. Newspapers at first gave little credit to the two Black men who had led part of the rescue, an injustice that Morgan spoke about for years.

Morgan's best-known idea came from the street. In the early 1920s, Cleveland's roads were crowded with cars, horse-drawn wagons, bicycles, and people on foot, and many traffic signals of the day switched from stop to go with no warning in between. According to many accounts, Morgan designed a signal after seeing a bad collision at an intersection. His signal had an extra position that stopped traffic in every direction for a moment before the signal changed. He received a patent for it in 1923 and later sold the rights to General Electric.

That brief pause, a moment when everyone waits, serves the same purpose as the warning light in the signals we use today.
